en: The Jātaka:
The Twelfth Chapter,
The Section on the Lesser Kuṇāla.
8. The Meṇḍaka Question Jātaka:
“For those among whom friendship has never before existed, even for as long as seven steps in this world;”
“Two friends have been born as enemies;
for what reason do they wander about in opposition?
“If today, at the time of my morning meal...”
“You would not have been able to answer this question;
I shall banish you all from the kingdom,
for I have no need for those of such poor wisdom.”
“In that terrible gathering of the great multitude,
when a tumultuous clamor of people had arisen,
my mind was distracted and my thoughts were manifold.”
We are not able to state this question.
Each one of us, with a one-pointed mind,
having gone into seclusion, has reflected upon the matter.
“Having fully understood solitude, O Lord of Men, the wise ones will then declare this matter:
‘[This is] for the sons of noble families and the daughters of kings.’”
The flesh of the ram is dear and pleasing;
they do not give that flesh to the dog,
yet the dog has friendship with the ram.
“They beat the skin of a sheep for the sake of the comfort of a horse-horse-back rug,
yet they do not spread it for a dog.”
“Then let there be friendship between this ram and the dog.
“For the ram has curved horns,
while the dog has no horns at all.”
"One who eats grass and one who eats meat—
how can there be friendship between a ram and a dog?
"The ram eats grass and eats leaves," [he replied].
The dog does not eat grass nor the palāśa leaf;
the dog might seize a hare or a cat,
but there can be no friendship between the dog and the ram.
“The ram, with eight-and-a-half feet,
four legs, and eight hooves, remains invisible;
he brings fodder for this one while hiding himself.”
This one brings meat for him.
Having gone to his excellent palace,
the best of the Videhas observes the exchange of various foods.
The Lord of Men indeed witnessed with his own eyes this state of Bubhukka, whose face was full of joy:
"Truly, my gains are of no small measure!"
In whose family there are wise ones,
those steadfast ones who, by means of well-spoken words, penetrate the subtle and profound meaning of a question.
One hundred horses and one chariot each,
and one excellent, prosperous village each—
I give all these to you, O wise ones.
“With a mind that has transcended the Supreme, through well-spoken words.
Thus ends the eighth Jātaka, the Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka.
